subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 24-year-old man has a painless cervical lymph node. Biopsy shows large bilobed tumor giant cells whose two nuclei are mirror images of each other, giving an owl-eye appearance, set in an inflammatory background. The findings confirm Hodgkin lymphoma.
question: What is the expected immunophenotype of these neoplastic cells?

options.text: CD3+ and CD4+, with a T-cell origin.
CD20+ and CD10+, with a germinal center B-cell origin.
CD15+ and CD30+, with a B-cell origin.
CD138+ and CD38+, with a plasma cell origin.
CD34+ and TdT+, with an immature blast origin.

explanation_correct: Reed-Sternberg cells are the distinctive tumor giant cells of Hodgkin lymphoma, with bilobed nuclei whose halves are mirror images, the classic owl-eye morphology. They express CD15 and CD30 and are of B-cell origin despite the paucity of mature B-cell markers. A useful mnemonic is two owl eyes times 15 equals 30. This immunophenotype is central to confirming the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: CD3 and CD4 are T-cell markers; Reed-Sternberg cells are not T cells even though rare T-cell lineage cases exist.
explanation_incorrect.B: CD20 and CD10 mark germinal center B cells; Reed-Sternberg cells typically lack strong CD20 and are defined by CD15 and CD30.
explanation_incorrect.D: CD138 and CD38 are plasma cell markers, associated with plasma cell dyscrasias rather than Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: CD34 and TdT mark immature blasts as in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, not the mature giant cells of Hodgkin lymphoma.

educationalObjective: Reed-Sternberg cells are CD15+/CD30+ tumor giant cells of B-cell origin with classic owl-eye bilobed nuclei.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma. Biopsy shows bands of collagen fibrosis dividing the node into nodules, with lacunar variants of Reed-Sternberg cells. She has no known immunodeficiency and has localized mediastinal and cervical disease.
question: Which subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma is most likely?

options.text: Nodular sclerosis.
Mixed cellularity.
Lymphocyte-rich.
Lymphocyte-depleted.
Nodular lymphocyte-predominant.

explanation_correct: Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma. It is characterized by collagen bands that subdivide the lymph node into nodules and by lacunar Reed-Sternberg cells, and it commonly affects young adults with mediastinal or cervical disease. The described histology fits this subtype directly.

explanation_incorrect.B: Mixed cellularity is associated with prominent eosinophilia and immunocompromised patients rather than collagen-banded nodules.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lymphocyte-rich Hodgkin lymphoma has abundant lymphocytes with only scattered Reed-Sternberg cells and the best prognosis, not the fibrotic nodular pattern.
explanation_incorrect.D: Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin lymphoma has few lymphocytes, many Reed-Sternberg cells, and the worst prognosis, typically in immunocompromised patients.
explanation_incorrect.E: Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma is a rare, indolent form with lymphocyte-predominant nodules and is not the most common subtype.

educationalObjective: Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by collagen bands and lacunar Reed-Sternberg cells.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 55-year-old man with a history of HIV infection presents with lymphadenopathy, fever, and weight loss. Biopsy of a lymph node shows Reed-Sternberg cells in a background with marked eosinophilia. Staging reveals widespread disease.
question: Which subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma is most consistent with these findings?

options.text: Nodular sclerosis, the most common subtype, with collagen bands and lacunar cells.
Lymphocyte-rich disease, with the best prognosis and only scattered Reed-Sternberg cells.
Lymphocyte-depleted disease, with a paucity of lymphocytes and numerous Reed-Sternberg cells.
Nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease, a rare indolent form with lymphocyte-rich nodules.
Mixed cellularity, which is associated with eosinophilia and seen in immunocompromised patients.

explanation_correct: Mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma is the subtype associated with prominent eosinophilia and is seen in immunocompromised patients, such as those with HIV infection. This patient's combination of immunodeficiency, eosinophil-rich infiltrate, and Reed-Sternberg cells fits mixed cellularity. It tends to present with more widespread disease and B symptoms.

explanation_incorrect.A: Nodular sclerosis is defined by collagen bands and lacunar cells and is not specifically linked to eosinophilia or HIV-associated disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Lymphocyte-rich Hodgkin lymphoma has the best prognosis and few Reed-Sternberg cells; it is not characterized by eosinophilia or immunocompromise.
explanation_incorrect.C: Although lymphocyte-depleted disease also occurs in immunocompromised patients, it is defined by lymphocyte depletion and numerous Reed-Sternberg cells rather than eosinophilia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma is rare and indolent and does not match the eosinophil-rich, immunocompromised presentation.

educationalObjective: Mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with eosinophilia and occurs in immunocompromised patients.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A pathology report compares two cases of Hodgkin lymphoma. Case 1 shows a lymph node enriched in lymphocytes with only scattered Reed-Sternberg cells. Case 2 shows a depleted lymph node with numerous Reed-Sternberg cells and little remaining lymphoid tissue.
question: Which pairing of subtype and prognosis is correct?

options.text: Case 1 is nodular sclerosis (best prognosis); Case 2 is mixed cellularity (worst prognosis).
Case 1 is lymphocyte-rich (best prognosis); Case 2 is lymphocyte-depleted (worst prognosis).
Case 1 is lymphocyte-depleted (worst prognosis); Case 2 is lymphocyte-rich (best prognosis).
Case 1 is mixed cellularity (worst prognosis); Case 2 is nodular sclerosis (best prognosis).
Both cases are nodular sclerosis, which has an intermediate prognosis.

explanation_correct: Lymphocyte-rich Hodgkin lymphoma has the best prognosis, with abundant lymphocytes and only scattered Reed-Sternberg cells, matching Case 1. Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin lymphoma has the worst prognosis, with few lymphocytes and numerous Reed-Sternberg cells, matching Case 2. The mnemonic is that the rich have better bank accounts and the poor have worse bank accounts.

explanation_incorrect.A: Nodular sclerosis has an intermediate-to-good prognosis and mixed cellularity does not carry the worst prognosis; the histology also does not fit.
explanation_incorrect.C: This reverses the two cases: the lymphocyte-rich node has the best, not the worst, prognosis and the depleted node the worst.
explanation_incorrect.D: Mixed cellularity is not the worst-prognosis subtype and nodular sclerosis is not the best; the described cellularity does not match either case.
explanation_incorrect.E: The two cases have distinctly different histologies and prognoses, so they cannot both be nodular sclerosis.

educationalObjective: Lymphocyte-rich Hodgkin lymphoma has the best prognosis, whereas lymphocyte-depleted disease has the worst.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: An epidemiologic review of Hodgkin lymphoma notes two distinct peaks in incidence: one in young adulthood and a second after age 55. Cases in young adults frequently show Epstein-Barr virus within Reed-Sternberg cells. The researchers propose an explanation for these observations.
question: Which of the following best explains the epidemiologic pattern described?

options.text: Hodgkin lymphoma has a unimodal distribution confined to childhood and is linked to HTLV-1 infection.
The disease occurs almost exclusively after age 70 and is caused by chronic Helicobacter pylori infection.
The two peaks reflect two entirely separate diseases, one of which is actually non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal age distribution with peaks in young adults and after age 55, and it is associated with EBV.
The second peak after age 55 is entirely attributable to improved screening, with no true rise in incidence.

explanation_correct: Hodgkin lymphoma shows a characteristic bimodal age distribution, with one peak in young adults and a second peak in patients older than 55 years. It is associated with Epstein-Barr virus, and EBV-positive Reed-Sternberg cells are frequently found, especially in younger patients. These two features together account for the observed epidemiology. This contrasts with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which can occur at any age and is linked to other viral and autoimmune conditions.

explanation_incorrect.A: The distribution is bimodal rather than unimodal or confined to childhood, and HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell lymphoma, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hodgkin lymphoma is not confined to patients older than 70, and H pylori is linked to marginal zone MALT lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.C: Both peaks represent Hodgkin lymphoma; they do not correspond to two different diseases or to non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: The older-age peak reflects a genuine increase in disease incidence, not merely ascertainment bias from screening.

educationalObjective: Hodgkin lymphoma shows a bimodal age distribution with peaks in young adults and after age 55 and is associated with EBV infection.
